drills.q: Explain the difference between sustained-use and committed-use discounts, and which current-generation machine families get neither automatically.
drills.a: SUDs are automatic, commitment-free, ramp with monthly usage (up to 30%/20% depending on family). CUDs require a 1- or 3-year commitment, billed whether used or not, for up to 55-70% (resource-based) or 28-46% (compute flexible). SUD eligibility is frozen at N1/N2/N2D/C2/M1/M2/sole-tenant/N1-GPUs -- newer families like E2, C3, C4, N4, H3, Z3 get zero automatic SUD regardless of runtime; only a CUD discounts them.

drills.q: A team purchases a 1-year compute flexible CUD expecting savings on their M2 (memory-optimized) fleet. What happens?
drills.a: Nothing -- compute flexible CUDs give 0% discount on memory-optimized series at the 1-year term; spend still burns down the commitment with no discount applied. Only a 3-year compute flexible commitment unlocks a discount (63%) on memory-optimized spend. A resource-based CUD avoids this since it offers up to 70% off M-series at both 1yr and 3yr terms.

drills.q: Explain GKE Autopilot's two billing models and what determines which applies to a given Pod.
drills.a: General-purpose Pods (default platform or Balanced/Scale-Out classes) get Pod-based billing: charged for the resource request in 1-second increments, no minimum. Pods requesting specific hardware (GPU, named machine series) switch to node-based billing: Autopilot provisions a real node sized to fit the request (possibly larger) and bills for the whole node plus a management premium.

drills.q: What is the GKE cluster management fee and does the free tier cover regional clusters?
drills.a: A flat $0.10/cluster/hour applies to every GKE cluster regardless of mode or topology. The $74.40/month free-tier credit covers roughly one zonal Standard or Autopilot cluster's fee, but explicitly does NOT apply to regional cluster management fees or compute charges.

drills.q: When would you choose GKE Standard over Autopilot for a new workload, given Google's Autopilot-first default guidance?
drills.a: When the workload needs privileged containers/hostPath access, custom DaemonSets beyond Autopilot's limits, fine-grained node-level tuning, or specific GPU/TPU node topologies requiring direct node control. For most stateless-to-moderately-stateful workloads without these needs, Autopilot is the better default.

drills.q: Design the compute discount strategy for a steady-state 3+ year core platform vs a rapidly machine-type-changing ML training fleet.
drills.a: Steady-state platform on an SUD-eligible family (e.g. N2): SUD automatically plus a resource-based 3-year CUD for up to 55% off, since the machine type genuinely won't change. Volatile ML fleet: a compute flexible CUD (28-46% depending on term) since it doesn't pin machine type or region, avoiding the stranding risk a resource-based commitment would carry if hardware needs shift quarterly.

drills.q: A FinOps review finds SUD credits dropped sharply the month a project moved between Cloud Billing accounts. Explain why.
drills.a: Sustained resource usage time is tracked per Cloud Billing account, not per project independent of account. Moving a project resets usage time to zero in the new account -- it isn't carried forward -- so the transition month sees a temporary drop in effective SUD rate. Mitigation: time billing account changes for the first day of a month.

drills.q: Compare GKE Autopilot's Pod-based billing to Fargate's task billing and explain the difference in incentives.
drills.a: Fargate bills continuously per provisioned vCPU/memory for however long a task runs, regardless of actual load fluctuation. Autopilot bills per-Pod resource request in 1-second increments with no minimum, only while the Pod is Running or being created -- both charge for requested/provisioned capacity rather than measured consumption, but Autopilot's finer granularity and stricter 'no billing for unscheduled/terminated Pods' rule link cost more tightly to actual workload lifecycle.

drills.q: Why can't resource-based CUDs be canceled, and what operational discipline does that require?
drills.a: The deep discount (up to 55-70%) is priced specifically on the customer committing to pay regardless of usage; allowing cancellation would undermine that pricing basis. Required discipline: forecast conservatively before committing, prefer compute flexible CUDs for anything with machine-type/region uncertainty, and use commitment merge/split/upgrade tooling (the only real adjustment levers) rather than assuming cancellation is possible.

drills.q: A GKE Standard node pool shows 35% CPU utilization. Is migrating to Autopilot with tightly-tuned requests guaranteed to reduce cost?
drills.a: No. If 35% reflects pool-level over-provisioning fixable via smaller machine types or better autoscaler tuning on Standard itself, savings might be achievable without migrating. Migration clearly wins only when the root cause is per-Pod over-requesting that Standard's shared-pool model was masking -- diagnose the root cause before defaulting to a platform migration, which carries its own compatibility risk (Autopilot's stricter security defaults).
